control.title: Technique: Day Under Control
control.description: This article introduces the unique “Two-Column” planning technique, designed to improve self-organization and boost personal effectiveness. You’ll learn how simply splitting tasks into “plans” and “facts” can help you not only achieve your goals but also reflect on your daily actions. We’ll focus on analyzing what you’ve actually accomplished, helping you learn how to adapt to changes and find a balance between what you need to do and what you want to do.

texts: <activitylink id="lsafnanS3sf">
The first exercise we want to share with you is simple yet effective, and it will help with your self-organization.
In the evening, before the next day begins, sit down and write out your schedule. It will consist of two parts, and therefore, two columns.
The first column is “Before.” This is an hourly plan of what you want to do. Don’t write too much at once: in each hourly slot, just write one or two words to denote an activity or action.

For example, it could be something small, like taking a shower, having breakfast, or starting a load of laundry. Or it could be something more demanding, such as cleaning, studying for an exam, or writing a resume.
At the end of each day, fill in the second column — “After.”
Use this column to record what you actually did throughout the day, also on an hourly basis. Your activities might match your plans, or they might differ — that’s perfectly fine, so don’t worry.
<important>Even if you only manage to complete a small part of your “Before” list, the simple act of planning your time can be a very helpful and visually clear process for you.</important>
mark any activity with the letter “D” (for Deed) if that task was difficult for you and felt like a specific accomplishment.

When dealing with depression, things like brushing your teeth or taking a shower might feel like a real achievement; believe me, there is nothing wrong or shameful about that. In those cases, you would write the letter “A” next to the task. You should also note the level of difficulty.
For example, if making the bed was quite easy, you might write “D-2,” but if cooking lunch was harder, it might be “D-7.” You decide the scale based on how you feel.
If an activity in your plan was enjoyable, mark it with “U” for “Unforgettable pleasure” or simply “U” to match the original symbol.
For instance, if watching a movie or walking in the park brought you joy, mark it with the corresponding letter and rate the level of pleasure you derived from the activity.
That is essentially the whole exercise: it’s simple but effective. You might think it won’t work, but you won’t know for sure unless you give it a try regularly for a while. It works because:
• It stops you from constantly overthinking the importance or value of certain actions and helps you manage internal conflicts about whether or not you should do something;
• It helps you plan your time in a balanced way, as it includes both necessary tasks and activities that bring you pleasure;

If you keep a daily schedule regularly, you will soon notice your motivation growing. By starting to do even small things, you will begin to challenge the belief that you are incapable of doing anything.
One person who struggled with long-term depression and procrastination shared their feedback on this technique:
<dialog man="true">By planning my day and looking at the results in the evening, I realized exactly where my time was going.</dialog>
<dialog man="true">It helped me take responsibility for my life again. I realize that I can control the situation if I choose to.</dialog>
<q author="Peter Drucker">The most important thing in time management is not to manage time, but to manage yourself</q>

death.title: Finding Yourself After the Loss of a Loved One
death.description: This article tells the story of Anastasia, who experienced deep depression and intense guilt following the tragic death of her brother. Through psychotherapy, she was able to gradually let go of self-blame, change how she viewed herself and her experiences, and eventually emerge from depression, accepting that she was not to blame and beginning to live a full life again.

texts: Sooner or later, each of us faces the loss of a loved one. Death is a profound trial that can overwhelm you with pain and heaviness, like a powerful wave.
Tears, sadness, and deep emotions are natural reactions to loss. These experiences help us process grief and find the strength to keep moving forward.
Sometimes grief becomes prolonged and can stay with a person for years. At other times, it can rapidly escalate into deep depression.
Let’s look at the story of Anastasia, a 29-year-old woman who faced severe depression after her younger brother’s suicide. She sought help from a psychologist a few months after the tragedy.
A particularly painful factor was her belief that she was responsible for his death.
<q author="Confucius">Those we love may leave us, but they never go far as long as we remember them.</q>
Anastasia felt as though she were facing an unsolvable and terrifying reality. She felt she “deserved” to suffer and even experienced suicidal thoughts.
Guilt is a common and heavy companion for those who have lost a loved one, especially if the person passed away by their own choice.
Many people ask themselves: “Why didn’t I stop this? Why didn’t I notice it in time?”

<important>Even experienced professionals can struggle with such thoughts if a client dies by suicide: “It really is my fault. I should have said something else, asked differently, been more attentive. I should have prevented this. It’s my fault!”</important>

Anastasia’s self-blame began even before the tragedy. She often felt her life had turned out better than her brother’s, and she tried to support him both emotionally and financially during his long struggle with depression.
She encouraged him to see a psychologist, helped pay for his therapy, and even rented an apartment near him so she could be close and always be there to help.
Anastasia was convinced she was to blame for his death because she “should have done even more.”
Her feelings were deep and sincere; she felt this pain constantly.

During her first therapy sessions, she spoke about the reasons for her self-blame and her thoughts about death: “I was responsible for his life. I feel like my inability to help led to this tragedy. I should have seen his state and saved him.”
She believed her suffering was justified and that she was obligated to carry the punishment.
From the outside, it can be clear that such thoughts are irrational and only cause harm.
The main cognitive distortion she was experiencing was personalization. Through therapy, Anastasia reached several important conclusions:
• If she had truly been responsible for her brother’s death, it would mean she was the cause of his decision.
• She could not control his thoughts or his internal pain, so she could not be responsible for the beliefs that led him into deep depression. It was his struggle, not her fault.
• By trying to take responsibility for his condition, she was trying to influence things beyond her control. The most she could do was support him within her own limits and abilities.
• If she had known his intentions, she would have done everything possible to help and prevent the tragedy. But she didn’t know—and it was impossible to change what was hidden.
• By blaming herself, Anastasia was acting as if she were required to foresee the future and possess limitless knowledge. These expectations were unrealistic, and she had no reason to blame herself.
All the evidence pointed to one thing: taking responsibility for his actions was a heavy and unfair mistake.
Her responsibility was only to her own life and her own well-being.
Over time, she realized that her suffering didn’t stem from “letting her brother down,” but from letting guilt consume her and allowing depression to destroy her life.
A supportive step was to let go of the guilt, gradually recover, and learn to live a joyful, fulfilling life again.

This is what true self-care looks like. After therapy, Anastasia’s condition improved significantly, and she was able to overcome her depression. She attributed this to deep changes in how she viewed herself and her inner world.

diagnostic.title: Understanding Depression: A Journey to Self-Discovery
diagnostic.description: The article covers various ways to diagnose depression, from recognizing general symptoms to self-assessment using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). It emphasizes the importance of seeking professional help for an accurate diagnosis and support, especially when symptoms are severe, and offers practical steps and exercises for those who want to care for their emotional well-being.

texts: In the previous section, we discussed what depression is.
Now, let’s look at how you can identify it in yourself.
Identifying depression generally involves three stages:
General screening
Like any other emotional state, depression manifests through specific symptoms. Let’s look at them:
• Low mood.
• Loss of interest in activities you used to enjoy.
• Anhedonia — a reduced ability to experience pleasure.
• Difficulty concentrating, working, or making decisions.
• Changes in sleep or appetite — either a decrease or an increase.
• Feelings of hopelessness, helplessness, irritability, shame, or guilt.
• Anxiety or profound apathy.
• Low energy or a constant feeling of fatigue.
• Intrusive thoughts about death or suicide.
Many of us have experienced some of these symptoms at least once.
However, experiencing individual symptoms doesn’t always mean you have depression. So, how can you tell?
A depressive disorder may be considered if you observe at least four of these symptoms for two weeks or longer.
It is also important to consider your overall health and the impact of your current life circumstances.
<q author="Viktor Frankl">We cannot change the situations life presents to us, but we can change how we experience them.</q>
Self-assessment using proven methods
There are many tools available to help you assess how you’re feeling.
One of the most well-known and reliable is the “Beck Depression Inventory” (BDI).
Developed by psychotherapist Aaron Beck, this method includes 21 items, each reflecting different aspects of a depressive state.
By taking this test, you can get an idea of the severity of your symptoms, ranging from mild to severe depression.
The test is available in our app and is simple and intuitive to use.
<q author="Lennard Davis">Self-care is not an exception to your responsibilities, but an important part of them.</q>
Consultation with a specialist
If your self-assessment results suggest possible depression, it’s important to reach out to a psychologist, psychiatrist, or psychotherapist.
A specialist can help clarify a diagnosis and find the right support and treatment plan. We’re here to support you and provide helpful information along the way.
This material is designed to support people experiencing mild to moderate symptoms of depression.
However, it can also be beneficial for those facing more severe conditions.
It can help ease symptoms and provide a better understanding of what you’re going through. However, for severe depression, self-help tools alone may not be enough.
In such cases, it is especially important to seek professional help and, if necessary, consider medical support.
<important>Diagnosing emotional states is a delicate and complex process.</important>
There is always a risk of error when assessing yourself.
Even if you don’t have clinical depression but are just experiencing a temporary low mood, this section can still be helpful.
We will explore the mechanisms of depression in detail and share practical recommendations and exercises.
If you want to improve your quality of life and are ready to take steps toward self-care, let’s continue this journey together.
